author: @blacklistnr1
text: But why make it slower to compute instead of just expanding the space of values? e.g. use something like 128 bytes (1024 bits) per hashed salted password, that to me sounds overkill enough that I wouldn't worry if the DB got leaked

author: @Kixunil
text: There are still ways to optimize speed without trashing security. First, if you have client-server architecture where the client uses the password to log in you can push hashing to the client and require 128-bit hash. Brute forcing anything 128-bit is impossible, so there's no vulnerability and the client being responsible for hashing decreases load on the server and potentially removes a DoS vulnerability.  Second, there was an interesting paper on a stretching algorithm that stretched the password as it was typed. Because typing the password takes time between the key strokes they used this to squeeze in some stretching. So to the user it looked faster even though it really took the same or even longer time.

author: @christopherg2347
text: The downside is that salting is a bit tricky that way. You basically have to do a 2 step process where inputting the username already retrieves the salting string. Which also could leak that a specific user name exists. On the plus side it does mean you aren't sending a clear text password over the Internet anymore.

author: @exscape
text: This problem has gotten a bit worse recently with monitors that don't use the RGB stripe subpixel layout, most notably OLED monitors. W-OLED panels typically use 4 subpixels (still in the vertical stripe layout), adding a white: previously RWBG, more recently RGWB as that works better with the old text rendering algorithms. QD-OLED monitors don't use the stripe layout at all, but rather a triangular layout, with the green subpixel on top, and red/bottom on the bottom. Since Windows assumes the RGB stripe layout is being used, it fails to correctly position the subpixels.  Just now (in 2026) both W-OLED and QD-OLED monitors with standard RGB stripe layout are on their way onto the market; I think some have launched by now, so this is finally about to be "solved" and back to normal for people buying the latest monitors.

author: @krystiano.610
text: Most of the time, colored text isn't the issue with the subpixel aa, but with the color mode negotiated between the GPU and the monitor. If monitor uses high refresh rate and / or high resolution - then with cheaper cables there may not be enough bandwidth to use full RGB color for pixels. Encoded color is then used - YCbCr, you can search more about this when looking at chroma subsampling, but oversimplifying - it's a lossy compression method for the display

author: @T33K3SS3LCH3N
text: 2:00 If anyone is wondering how anti-aliasing works in 3D if it's already so complex in 2D:  Most 3D anti-aliasing (AA) methods use super sampling, which means that they actually calculate more pixels than the output image has.   4x SSAA means that the image simply gets renderered at 4x the output resolution, and then each output pixel is the average of 4 pixels.  Because that's horribly inefficient to do, MSAA (Multi-Sample AA) was invented. It first detects which pixels contain the border between two different objects (which can be done relatively efficiently), and then only performs SSAA on those pixels. It's still quite slow though, especially if you have a lot of borders (like if there is a lot of thin, fine detail like hair strands, wire fences, lots of plants or particle effects...).  This is why most modern games use Temporal AA (TAA), which can also work as an upscaler (DLSS/Deep-Learning Super Sampling is a TAA algorithm).  TAA is super sampling across time. It only calculates one colour per pixel per frame, but it does so from a different point within each pixel every frame. It then uses motion vectors (one vector per pixel which show where the thing in that pixel was during the last frame) to stitch these multiple samples per pixel from successive frames together. So after 4 frames, you can have 4 samples per pixel a d therefore either have 4x SSAA or can upscale the output image to 4x the resolution (DLSS aims for something like 16 samples per pixel at 2x upscaling, so it can do upscaling and AA).  So basically, 3d AA relies on the brute force of just calculating more pixels, but it has become really smart about how it does that.

author: @dedr4m
text: Fun fact, the old way was to use a character map in video memory or character ROM, a character would be given an address, when the scanline went past, it'd iterate through the same table of addresses (80 addresses for an 80 character long row) until it reached the last line of the character and produced a number of blanks specified either by the mapping ROM or the main ROM (for x86, the BIOS/vBIOS), then it did the same for the next 25 rows, hence the 80x25 character video mode. It was quick and efficient because, rather than doing calculations over and over, simply the ROM would have the address of the character referenced, then the ROM would be on the databus instead of the CPU/GPU thus what bits were set at the address would then show up on screen as it drew them. There were many ways to make a character map, some meant that each row of the character would be offset for 16 times by 8-bits at the starting address (hence the 8 by 16 characters in old computers, especially x86), the other was to have 255 characters in a ROM and offset each address by 255 to get to the next row, easier to visualise but hard to do in practice. The techniques changed over time, like using sprite hardware to manage text instead (though, technically, the old character ROM technique, of the memory mapped type, was able to be mapped out and technically be used to make sprites). text: 4:38 I made an Android music app, and I was optimizing performance of a specific function. Would you know what ? the text_render native function topped the chart on CPU use. The audio thread use was tiny, didn't even appear. And the absurd amount of binder calls to the Surface Flinger, 2 per frame per second. The audio didn't even do any binder calls after setting the channel, it doesn't have a "v-sync", it just uses a shared-memory file descriptor sent once. Everything else is native code, and runs in 100 microseconds, one can use at most 16 milliseconds to draw at 60 fps. At 80 microseconds, that's a "frame-rate" of 10000 audio frames, way above the 50 required for 960 samples per frame to get 48000Khz.  Thank God I don't have to write a darned text renderer.
